conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain in my belly for a few days now, worse than before. It goes to my back too. I threw up 12 times yesterday and had diarrhea 10 times. I feel dizzy when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you had a TACE procedure recently for liver cancer. Any headaches or falls since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had bad headaches like migraines. I think I fell after my last hospital stay and hit my left eye, but I don’t remember much. No vision changes though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting me know. We’ll keep an eye on that. Your blood pressure was high in the ER, but it’s better now. We’re giving you IV fluids because your lactate was high, which means you were dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak? I haven’t been drinking much, and I had two drinks three days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We also gave you some diazepam because stopping alcohol suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms. That might help your stomach pain too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t know that could affect my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen. Your liver looks like it has cirrhosis, which we expected, and the spot from your TACE procedure hasn’t changed. No new tumors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? No new cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s good news. The appendix is a bit swollen but hasn’t changed from past scans, so it’s likely not the cause. No signs of infection in your blood or stool either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it could be from withdrawing from alcohol, or maybe from stopping certain medications like oxycodone or benzodiazepines. Those can cause stomach cramps when you stop them suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did take oxycodone for pain, but only when it got really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to slowly reduce that while you’re here. Narcotics can actually make abdominal symptoms worse over time. We’ll use other ways to manage your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my liver meds? I haven’t been taking the lactulose regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your lactulose, rifaximin, and spironolactone. They’re important for your liver. The diarrhea you had might be from restarting the lactulose, but it should settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been skipping it because it upsets my stomach sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. We also placed a small tube in your neck vein to make giving IV fluids and meds easier. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels strange, but I guess it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your lactate has improved—from 5.8 down to 1.5—thanks to the fluids. Your liver numbers are stable, and your infection tests came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Stool tests were negative for C. diff, Salmonella, and Campylobacter. Blood cultures are still pending but no signs of fever or worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? It’s better but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on a new medicine called hyoscyamine. It helps with cramping. Since your pain improved with diazepam, we think it’s related to withdrawal, so we’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send it home with you—take it as needed for cramping. We’re also continuing your thiamine, folate, and B12 for your nutrition and liver health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been feeling anxious too. Is that part of withdrawal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can be. We’re keeping you on your quetiapine for mood and sleep. We’ll avoid benzodiazepines going forward since they can worsen withdrawal symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your blood counts are low, which we knew from before. But they’re stable—no bleeding or new issues. Your liver function is unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my liver or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely from your cirrhosis. We’ll keep monitoring. Your MELD score is 14, which means your liver is moderately affected, but not urgent for transplant right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because of the drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Staying alcohol-free is important if transplant becomes an option. But for now, we’re focused on getting your symptoms under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to stop. It’s just hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help with that. We’ll connect you with counseling and support. For now, you’re doing well—no more vomiting, and your pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your symptoms have improved, labs are stable, and you’re tolerating food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your liver meds, especially lactulose. Use hyoscyamine for cramps. Avoid alcohol, oxycodone, and benzos. If you have fever, severe pain, or vomiting, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with your hepatologist and primary care doctor. We’ll also send a note to your psychiatrist. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel a lot better.
